speaker: Kimi K3
text: PNB's Q1 net income jumped to Rs 58.1 bn from Rs 21.2 bn a year ago, so the 25.5% five-year CAGR isn't just a low-base bounce -- earnings are actually compounding. The 4.76% dividend yield covers most of your 0.38% round-trip cost on Zerodha delivery, and at 6.2x trailing earnings the stock still trades below book value despite the clean-up. For the US side, $100 in fractional NVDA at today's $214 would buy ~0.467 shares; at the 25.2% 5-year CAGR that grows to ~$125 in a year, not $1,000 -- you'd need roughly 63% annual returns to 10x in 12 months, which only lottery tickets deliver. On the IPO question: with $10 you can't meet the typical $150-250 minimum lot on US platforms, and Indian IPOs need a PAN-linked demat account, so park the cash in a high-yield money-market fund (currently ~4.5%) until you have the Rs 15k minimum lot size.

The best bet is to park the cash in a high‑yield money‑market fund or a short‑term bond ETF until you hit the minimum lot size.  For Reliance (RELIANCE.NS) on Zerodha, delivery brokerage is zero, but you’ll pay a Rs 15.93 DP fee plus the standard 0.38 % total charges (STT, SEBI, stamp duty, GST, exchange fee).  That’s about 0.4 % of the trade value, so a Rs 10,000 purchase costs roughly Rs 40 in fees.  If you’re interested in car and battery makers, look at Maruti Suzuki (MARUTI.NS), Tata Motors (TATAMOTORS.NS) and battery names like Exide Industries (EXIDEIND.NS) or Amara Raja (AMARAJAA.NS); they’re all listed on NSE and can be bought in whole shares.  Keep in mind the 20 % short‑term capital‑gain tax if you hold less than 12 months.

text: With a $10 US account you’re below the minimum lot size for most IPOs—most US IPOs require at least $1,000 in the first tranche, and Indian IPOs need a PAN‑linked demat and a lot size of at least ₹50,000, so you’d likely get nothing allotted. If you do get allotted, the broker will charge a small underwriting fee (typically 0.25‑0.5% of the allotment value) and a stamp duty of 0.5% on the purchase price; the broker’s commission is usually nil on IPOs. Buying Reliance (RELIANCE.NS) on Zerodha in a delivery account costs ₹20.00 STT, ₹0.59 exchange fee, ₹0.02 SEBI fee, ₹1.50 stamp duty, ₹0.11 GST, and a ₹15.93 DP charge, totaling about ₹38.15 on a ₹10,000 trade—roughly 0.38% of the value. For cars and battery makers, look at Maruti (MARUTI.NS) and Tata Motors (TATAMOTORS.NS) for auto, and Tata Power (TATAPOWER.NS) or Adani Energy (ADANIENT.NS) for batteries; their lot sizes and fees are similar to Reliance.
